reason: E1 directly supports the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer from an Hf coating and its oxidation resistance benefit, but it is on a refractory HEA, not boride-based components, and in oxidation, not molten-aluminum corrosion. E2 shows HfB2 has better oxidation resistance than other diborides in HEBs, but does not address Hf-rich surface treatments or molten-aluminum corrosion. The key premises about barrier protection against molten aluminum and in-situ conversion under hot-dip conditions lack direct evidence.
premises: Hf-rich coatings can form a dense, protective HfO2 layer upon high-temperature oxidation
Such HfO2 layers improve oxidation resistance and prevent surface degradation
HfB2 exhibits superior oxidation resistance among diborides in high-entropy boride ceramics
The protective HfO2 layer acts as a barrier to reduce substrate dissolution and corrosion
